findings.question: Can two initially identical neutral memories develop distinct roles under these deterministic updates?
findings.observation: Identically initialized neutral slots stayed identical; task-neutral random initial differences restored much of frozen B recall on the tested repeat/flip-like tasks.
findings.hypothesis: Symmetry prevents the two deterministic slots from specializing; random initialization can break that symmetry.
findings.next_test: Compare controlled symmetry-breaking mechanisms on fresh seeds and rule families, with equal prior strength and matched compute.
findings.limitations: The ablation also changed the persistent decay target, so initialization and decay effects were not isolated; tasks were public and synthetic.

findings.question: Does posterior-discounted plasticity improve the retention and switch tradeoff compared with the earlier predictive-gated candidate?
findings.observation: On matched 30-seed development and 30-seed separate-rule comparisons, idea 2 met all 12 non-inferiority checks; idea 1 met 8 and 9 respectively. Idea 2 had lower B recall than idea 1 in one unequal-noise development condition.
findings.hypothesis: Posterior-discounted learning can reduce interference while retaining enough adaptation on some rule families.
findings.next_test: Vary switch rate and task structure on matched seeds; separately compare update weights without altering inference.
findings.limitations: The rules were visible and hand-selected; both ideas modify an existing mixture. Non-inferiority does not demonstrate novelty or significance.

findings.question: Why does idea 2 lose B recall after A returns on the uneven-bias condition?
findings.observation: With 400 transitions per phase, frozen B recall for mixture and idea 2 was about 0.81 immediately after B; after A it was 0.786 and 0.686. In a post-hoc slot heuristic, 7/30 idea-2 runs crossed a 0.5 conditional-probability threshold and accounted for most of its average deficit.
findings.hypothesis: Updates during the final A phase may corrupt a B-like memory or its routing; the correlation does not identify a cause.
findings.next_test: Freeze or restore the identified memory after B and compare against a sham intervention on fresh paired seeds, measuring both B retention and A adaptation.
findings.limitations: The slot heuristic and threshold were selected post-hoc, ignore probe-time beliefs, and were measured on one public task; phase length also changes exposure.

findings.question: Does restoring the B-like slot contribute to final B recall on uneven-bias tasks?
findings.observation: Across 30 fresh seeds, restoring the selected slot after A returned raised mean B recall from 0.7278 to 0.8112 on uneven bias, but its median paired change was zero; on shifted bias the mean gain was 0.0148 and median change was -0.0065.
findings.hypothesis: Changes to the selected table can causally contribute to forgetting in some runs, but do not explain every failure or imply an online solution.
findings.next_test: Compare online slot protection against a matched sham or random-slot policy on fresh tasks and seeds, including adaptation and compute costs.
findings.limitations: This direct intervention restores a privileged end-of-B checkpoint and chooses a slot with a task-specific high-P(1) heuristic. Tasks are public, and the original hypothesis was post-hoc.

findings.question: Does freezing the less likely slot when predictive confidence exceeds 0.8 improve retention?
findings.observation: On 30 fresh paired seeds for uneven bias with 400-step phases, final B accuracy was 0.7233 with protection, 0.7543 for idea 2 and 0.7927 for the random-slot control. The protection policy froze a slot on 88.1% of steps; the random policy on 89.8%. On complementary 1000-step phases, protection scored 0.6161 versus idea 2 at 0.7006.
findings.hypothesis: A fixed high-confidence gate may freeze useful updates or become confident in the wrong assignment, but the measured suppression counts do not establish which mechanism caused the deficit.
findings.next_test: Inspect predictive beliefs and assignment accuracy around switches, compare narrower or learned protection only under a predeclared matched protocol, and avoid assuming every inactivity gate helps.
findings.limitations: Public synthetic tasks, one threshold, exploratory condition selection, unadjusted descriptive comparisons. Random control has independent beliefs and freezes on different steps; no matched compute.
